prompt.context: Your client is a carpet manufacturer that sells to both commercial and residential customers. Their current production process is: Buy dyed/pre-colored yarn → Load yarn spools in a specific order onto machine → Weave yarn into carpet → Run carpet through carpet backing machine → Cut, roll, and store the finished carpet. They are considering investing in a new technology that will cost $25M (initial investment). With the new technology, the production process will change to: Buy un-dyed yarn → Spool yarn → Weave yarn into carpet → Dye carpet through a printing process, much like an inkjet printer → Cut, roll, and store the finished carpet.
prompt.question: The client wants to know if they should invest in the new technology.

clarifying_info.q: Will the carpet made with the new technology be different in any way from the current product?
clarifying_info.a: The new carpet will have a better texture and can therefore be sold at a higher price point.

clarifying_info.q: How many yards of finished carpet are produced per year?
clarifying_info.a: 10 million yards of finished carpet per year.

clarifying_info.q: What is the useful life of the new machine?
clarifying_info.a: The new machine has a 10-year useful life.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost per yard of the original carpet?
clarifying_info.a: The cost per yard of the original carpet is $10/yard.

framework: Assess cost impact: how does switching to un-dyed yarn and inkjet dyeing change variable and fixed costs per yard?
Quantify cost savings vs. initial investment: compare NPV of savings over machine lifetime to $25M capex
Assess revenue impact: can the higher-quality carpet command a price premium and/or open new markets?
Consider cannibalization: will existing standard-carpet customers switch to the premium product?
Calculate net incremental revenue: incremental revenues minus incremental production costs
Evaluate investment feasibility: payback period, ROI, risks (market capture assumptions, ink cost volatility, maintenance)

questions.prompt: How would the new technology and process impact costs?
questions.guidance: Strong answers cover multiple cost dimensions: (1) Yarn costs decrease because un-dyed yarn is cheaper. (2) New cost for ink/dye. (3) Labor decreases since spools no longer need to be loaded by color. (4) New machine has different (potentially higher) maintenance requirements. (5) Electricity costs may increase. (6) One-time training costs. (7) Warehousing/inventory costs decrease because production can be made-to-order instead of forecasting color demand.

questions.prompt: Given that cost savings aggregate to $0.25 per finished yard, 10M yards produced per year, and a 10-year machine life, how would you value the investment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize the break-even math but also flag its limitations: time value of money means $25M in future savings is worth less than $25M today, so cost savings alone do not justify the investment. Must flag that incremental revenue potential needs to be explored.

math.setup: Annual savings = yards produced × savings per yard. Total savings over machine life = annual savings × useful life.
math.answer: $25M total savings equals the $25M machine cost at face value, but ignoring time value of money means the NPV of savings is actually less than $25M — cost savings alone do not justify the investment.

questions.prompt: The new carpet can be sold at $20/yard (a 25% premium over standard carpet). 30% of existing customers would upgrade to the new carpet. There is a 70M yard/year market for higher-quality carpet the client couldn't access before, and the client estimates capturing 5% of that market. What is the incremental revenue from introducing the high-quality carpet?
questions.guidance: Candidate must derive the standard carpet price from the premium percentage, calculate new volume mix, compute old vs. new revenues, and subtract. Standard carpet price = $20 / 1.25 = $16/yard. 30% of 10M existing yards cannibalized into premium = 3M yards premium from existing customers; remaining 7M yards stay standard. New market capture = 5% × 70M = 3.5M yards. Total premium yards = 3M + 3.5M = 6.5M yards.

math.setup: Standard price = premium price / 1.25. Old revenue = 10M yards × standard price. New revenue = standard yards × standard price + premium yards × premium price. Incremental revenue = new revenue − old revenue.
steps: Cannibalized standard yards: 30% × 10M = 3M yards move to premium; 7M yards remain standard
New market capture: 5% × 70M = 3.5M yards of premium

questions.prompt: Given a production cost of $10/yard for standard carpet and $9.75/yard for the new carpet (reflecting the $0.25/yard savings), what is the net incremental revenue after accounting for the additional production costs?
questions.guidance: Candidate must calculate old production costs on 10M yards, new production costs on the new volume mix (7M standard + 6.5M premium), find the incremental cost, then subtract from incremental revenue. The cost for the new carpet is $10 − $0.25 = $9.75/yard. The key insight is that total volume increases from 10M to 13.5M yards, so there are additional production costs that must be deducted.

math.setup: New carpet cost per yard = standard cost − savings per yard. Old production cost = 10M × $10. New production cost = 7M × $10 + 6.5M × $9.75. Net incremental costs = new − old. Net incremental revenue = incremental revenue − net incremental costs.

brainstorming.prompt: What would you want to validate or investigate further before finalizing the recommendation?

categories.name: Revenue assumptions
ideas: Validate the 30% cannibalization rate — is it based on customer research or a rough estimate?
Validate the 5% market capture estimate in the 70M yard premium market — how competitive is that market?
Assess whether the $20/yard price is sustainable given competitive dynamics
Consider whether commercial vs. residential mix affects willingness to pay the premium

categories.name: Cost assumptions
ideas: Confirm that the $0.25/yard savings figure is net of ink/dye costs
Analyze variability and cost trends for ink (commodity exposure)
Quantify maintenance costs for the new machine vs. existing equipment
Estimate one-time training and transition costs

categories.name: Investment risks
ideas: Time value of money: NPV of cost savings alone is less than $25M
Technology risk: is the inkjet dyeing technology proven at scale?
Operational risk: transition downtime could reduce production capacity
Market risk: premium carpet market may contract during economic downturns

categories.name: Strategic considerations
ideas: Can the client run both technologies in parallel to serve both segments?
Are competitors also considering this technology, creating urgency or first-mover advantage?
Supply chain implications of switching to un-dyed yarn suppliers
Flexibility benefit: made-to-order reduces inventory carrying costs and obsolescence risk

recommendation: Proceed with the $25M investment in the new inkjet dyeing technology
The investment is justified primarily by the revenue upside: $49M net incremental revenue per year against a $25M one-time cost implies a payback period of well under one year on an incremental basis
Cost savings alone ($2.5M/year) do not justify the investment on an NPV basis, but the revenue opportunity from entering the 70M yard premium market makes the investment highly attractive
risks: Market capture and cannibalization assumptions are estimates and could be materially off — if premium market capture is lower or cannibalization is higher, returns compress
Ink costs may be volatile or rise over time, eroding the $0.25/yard cost savings
Maintenance costs for the new technology may exceed expectations
Transition period could temporarily reduce output
next_steps: Conduct customer research to validate the 30% upgrade rate and willingness to pay $20/yard
Validate the 5% premium market capture assumption with a go-to-market plan
Analyze ink supplier contracts and cost structure to stress-test the $0.25/yard savings
Model NPV with a discount rate to confirm investment attractiveness on a time-adjusted basis
Assess transition plan to minimize production downtime during installation
